explanations.explanation: That's exactly what the text says. Mordecai walks in because Esther had revealed his relation to her. Esther's the queen, and she opens the door by saying who he is to her. Family connections still get you in the room, friend, even in a palace.

It's actually true, friend. The text says Mordecai entered the king's presence because Esther had revealed his relation to her. So the door opens because of what Esther told the king. Nobody had to pick a lock or knock down a wall.

Yes, the signet ring. The king had recovered it from Haman, the man who plotted against the Jews, and now he takes it off and presents it to Mordecai. A ring like that was how the king's name got stamped on things. That's a whole lot of trust to slide across the table, friend.

A gold chain is a good guess for a palace, but it's not what the text says. In this passage the king takes the signet ring he had recovered from Haman and presents it to Mordecai. No chain anywhere in these verses. I'd have kept looking in my pockets too.

I know that sounds royal, but no cup changes hands here. The text says the king removed the signet ring he had recovered from Haman and presented it to Mordecai. A cup holds a drink, friend, and this ring carried the king's name.

True. The text says Esther appointed Mordecai over the estate of Haman. The king gave her the estate, and she puts Mordecai over it. Mordecai raised her (Esther 2:7), and now she hands him the keys. I bet that felt good.
This one is true, friend. The text says Esther appointed Mordecai over the estate of Haman. The king had given her that estate, so she decides who runs it. That's the queen making her own call.

Right. She asks that an order be written to revoke the letters Haman wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces. Haman, the one who schemed against them, is gone, but his letters are still out there. She doesn't ask for something for herself, friend. She asks for her people.

explanations.answer: A royal guard for every Jew
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a solid plan, but it's not what she asks. Esther asks that an order be written to revoke the letters Haman had written to destroy the Jews. The problem is the letters themselves, still out in the provinces. A guard for everybody would be a lot of guards, friend.

Nope, she doesn't ask for that. Mordecai had already received the ring and the estate. What Esther asks for is an order to revoke the letters Haman wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces. She's keeping her eyes on the real problem.

Yes, destruction. Esther says, "How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?" She says it right after asking how she could bear to see the disaster befalling her people. You can hear it in her words, friend. This isn't a polite request anymore.

Exile is a real thing in the Bible, but it's not Esther's word here. She says, "How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?" Haman's letters were written to destroy the Jews, not to move them somewhere. That's a much bigger problem than a change of address, friend.

That would be hard, but it's not what she says. Esther says, "How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?" The letters Haman wrote were meant to destroy the Jews. Running low on money is rough, friend, and this is far beyond that.

explanations.answer: Write as they please in the king's name
explanations.explanation: That's it. The king tells them, "Now you may write in the king's name as you please regarding the Jews, and seal it with the royal signet ring." He's giving Esther and Mordecai the pen and the ring, friend. That's about as much freedom as a king can hand out.

explanations.answer: Burn every one of Haman's letters
explanations.explanation: Close to what Esther wanted, but that's not the king's answer. He says they may write in the king's name as they please regarding the Jews, and seal it with the royal signet ring. Haman's letters are already out in the provinces, so burning doesn't cover it. Nothing about a bonfire here, friend.

explanations.answer: Send soldiers to guard every Jew
explanations.explanation: That's not what the king says. He tells Esther and Mordecai, "Now you may write in the king's name as you please regarding the Jews, and seal it with the royal signet ring." The answer is a letter, friend, not a bunch of soldiers.

Careful, friend, the king says the opposite. He says, "For a decree that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the royal signet ring cannot be revoked." That's the whole reason Esther's problem is so tricky. Haman's letters were sealed that way, so they can't just be undone.

Yes, False. The king says, "For a decree that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the royal signet ring cannot be revoked." So Haman's sealed letters can't just be taken back. That's why the king hands Esther and Mordecai the pen and the ring instead.

Yes, Mordecai. The royal scribes recorded all of Mordecai's orders to the Jews and to the satraps, governors and princes. He's the one with the ring now, and these scribes are writing down what he says. I think those scribes got a serious hand cramp that day.

Harbonah shows up in this story, but not here. He's one of the eunuchs attending the king, and he speaks up about Haman's gallows (Esther 7:9). The scribes in this passage record all of Mordecai's orders. It's Mordecai's pen, so to speak, friend.

Hathach is in the story, but not in these verses. He's a eunuch the king assigned to attend Esther (Esther 4:5). Here, the royal scribes record all of Mordecai's orders. Mordecai is the one with the ring and the say-so, friend.

True. The scribes write to each province in its own script and to every people in their own language. The Jews get it in their own script and language too. Everybody gets the message in words they can actually read, friend.

This one is true, friend. The text says they wrote to each province in its own script, to every people in their own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language. So nobody has to squint at a letter they can't read. That's a lot of different handwriting for one scribe team.

That's it. Mordecai sends the documents by mounted couriers riding on swift horses bred from the royal mares. With that many provinces, you want speed. Those were the fastest delivery trucks they had, friend.

Runners are a fair guess, but the text says something faster. The documents go by mounted couriers riding on swift horses bred from the royal mares. Those couriers were on horseback, friend, not on foot. Your feet can rest.

Joppa was a real port, the city where Jonah found a ship (Jonah 1:3). But Mordecai doesn't use ships in these verses. He sends the documents by mounted couriers riding on swift horses bred from the royal mares. These letters travel by hoof, friend.

Yes. The king permitted the Jews in each and every city the right to assemble and defend themselves. Before this, Haman's letters had them with no way out. Now they're allowed to stand together, friend.

explanations.answer: To leave the kingdom in peace
explanations.explanation: That's not what the letters say. They give the Jews in each and every city the right to assemble and defend themselves. Nothing here tells them to pack up and go. They stay, and they stand together, friend.

explanations.answer: To hide inside the king's palace
explanations.explanation: I'd love a hiding spot that big, but no. The letters give the Jews in each and every city the right to assemble and defend themselves. That's in their own cities, friend. The palace is a long way from most of them.

explanations.answer: So the Jews will be ready on that day
explanations.explanation: Right. A copy of the edict was to be published to all the people, so that the Jews would be ready on that day. The day is set, and now they know about it ahead of time. Knowing the day is half of being ready, friend.

explanations.answer: So the king can count all his people
explanations.explanation: Nope, the text gives a different reason. The edict was published so that the Jews would be ready on that day. Nothing here says anything about a head count. That would be a lot of counting, friend.

explanations.answer: So every governor will send tribute
explanations.explanation: That's not it. The text says a copy of the edict was to be published to all the people, so that the Jews would be ready on that day. No tribute is mentioned in these verses. The purpose is being ready, friend.

True. Mordecai goes out from the king's presence in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen. This is the same Mordecai who walked in the front door only because Esther told the king who he was. Now he walks out looking like that, friend.

This is true, friend. The text says Mordecai went out in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen. Blue, white, gold and purple, all at once. That's a lot of outfit.
Not quite, friend. The text says the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced. Nobody is confused. They see Mordecai come out in his royal garments and they cheer.
Yes, False. The text says the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced when Mordecai came out. Nobody's scratching their head here. Susa is cheering, friend.

That's what the text says. Many of the people of the land themselves became Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them. The text gives that fear as the reason. That's a big turn from where this story started, friend.
Not here. The text says many of the people of the land themselves became Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them. They don't pack up and go. They join, friend.

explanations.answer: They rise up against the king
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says. Many of the people of the land themselves became Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them. Nothing here says anybody rises up against the king. They go the other direction, friend.
